en: Angry and bitter in speech or debate
hook: ACRIMONIOUS: ACRID, as bitter as acid.
story: Acrimonious. When Lamia's aunt and uncle divorced, nothing was peaceful. They shouted in the lawyer's office, insulted each other in court, and fought for months over every chair, spoon, and photograph. At family weddings, relatives seated them at opposite ends of the hall. The divorce was acrimonious: full of anger and bitterness. Acrid means sharp and bitter, like smoke. An acrimonious debate leaves both sides resentful long after it ends.

gre.s: What began as a friendly disagreement between the two scholars grew increasingly ____, until each was publicly accusing the other of fraud.
gre.clue: publicly accusing the other of fraud

example: The acrimonious split between the band's two founders played out for months in newspaper interviews and courtrooms.

en: Sharply severe or critical; also, causing skin tissue to contract
hook: ASTRINGENT: like a STRINGENT, tight squeeze, harsh.
story: Astringent. Arif sent his first novel manuscript to a famous editor. It came back three weeks later with comments in every margin: "Weak." "Lazy." "Cut this." "Why does this exist?" Not one kind word. Arif felt as if his skin had been scrubbed raw. The editor's comments were astringent: sharply severe and critical. Astringent lotions make skin pores contract and tighten. Astringent words make your whole stomach tighten.

gre.s: The critic's ____ reviews, which spared neither famous names nor beginners, made her the most feared voice in the literary world.
gre.clue: spared neither famous names nor beginners

example: Her astringent comments on the committee's draft, though painful to hear, saved the project from several costly errors.

en: Self-evident; accepted as true without proof
hook: AXIOM: a basic truth in math, needing no proof.
story: Axiomatic. In his first geometry class at university, Tanvir watched the professor write on the board: a straight line can be drawn between any two points. Tanvir raised his hand and asked for the proof. The professor smiled. 'There is none. We simply accept it, because it is obvious.' Such a statement is an axiom, and anything treated this way is axiomatic: self-evident, accepted as true without proof. In economics, it is almost axiomatic that people respond to incentives.

gre.s: It was once considered ____ that the sun revolved around the earth, a truth so plain that no one thought to question it, yet the assumption proved entirely false.
gre.clue: so plain that no one thought to question it

example: Among good cooks it is axiomatic that fresh ingredients matter more than any fancy technique.

en: To surrender or give in
hook: CAPITULATE: surrender your CAPITAL city.
story: Capitulate. For two weeks, students at a Dhaka college camped outside the administration building, demanding that a sudden fee increase be cancelled. The principal swore he would never give in. But as newspapers covered the protest and parents joined the students, he finally capitulated and announced that the increase was withdrawn. To capitulate is to surrender or give in, usually after resisting. It comes from a Latin word for drawing up terms under headings, like the chapters of a surrender treaty. Synonyms: yield, surrender, submit.

gre.s: After months of insisting that it would never negotiate, the management finally chose to ____ to the union's demands when the strike began to cripple production.
gre.clue: when the strike began to cripple production

example: After three hours of pleading from the twins, their mother capitulated and bought them ice cream before dinner.

en: To scold someone sharply for doing wrong
hook: CHASTISE: CHASE them with words until they're CHASTE (corrected).
story: Chastise. Tanvir came home at two in the morning after a friend's wedding, without calling anyone. His father was waiting in the drawing room. For twenty minutes he chastised Tanvir: how careless, how selfish, how worried his mother had been. Tanvir stared at the floor and said nothing. To chastise is to scold or criticize severely. It shares a root with chaste and chasten, from a Latin word meaning to make pure, as if the scolding cleans out the fault. Synonyms: rebuke, reprimand, castigate.

gre.s: Far from praising the minister's handling of the flood, the committee's report went out of its way to ____ him for delays that had cost lives.
gre.clue: Far from praising

example: The captain chastised her players for arriving late to training, reminding them that discipline wins tournaments.

en: Courteous, gallant, and honorable, especially toward women
hook: CHIVALROUS: like a medieval knight's CHIVALRY.
story: Chivalrous. The bus from Mirpur was packed. An elderly woman climbed on with heavy bags and nowhere to sit. A young man in a university T-shirt immediately stood up, offered her his seat, held her bags, and later helped her step down at her stop. Passengers smiled at each other. His behaviour was chivalrous: courteous, gallant, and honourable, especially toward women. The word comes from chivalry, the code of medieval knights.

gre.s: In an age of cynicism, the soldier's ____ treatment of his captured enemies, whom he fed and sheltered, astonished his comrades.
gre.clue: whom he fed and sheltered

example: In a chivalrous gesture, the champion helped his fallen opponent to his feet before raising his own arms in victory.

en: To damage someone's reputation with false statements
hook: DE-FAME: destroy someone's FAME.
story: Defame. A rival shopkeeper began telling customers that old Karim sold rotten fish dyed with chemicals. It was completely false, but Karim's sales dropped by half. He took the matter to court, where the rival was found guilty of trying to defame him: to damage his reputation with false statements. To defame is to take away someone's fame, their good name. The noun is defamation; spoken defamation is slander, and written defamation is libel. Synonyms: slander, libel, malign, smear.

gre.s: The politician's opponents sought to ____ him by spreading fabricated stories of corruption, hoping voters would believe the lies before they could be disproved.
gre.clue: spreading fabricated stories of corruption

example: The newspaper paid heavy damages after a court ruled that it had defamed a Sylhet surgeon with invented accusations.

en: Working well and producing the result that was wanted
hook: EFFICACIOUS: EFFECTIVE.
story: Efficacious. In the nineteen sixties and seventies, cholera and diarrhoea killed huge numbers of children in Bangladesh. Researchers in Dhaka helped show that a cheap drink of clean water, salt, and sugar could keep these children alive. Oral saline proved astonishingly efficacious: successful in producing the desired result. Efficacious is a formal word for effective, used mostly of treatments, methods, and policies. The noun is efficacy. Synonyms: effective, potent, successful. Opposite: ineffectual.

gre.s: The manufacturer touted the supplement as highly ____, yet independent trials showed that it relieved symptoms no better than a sugar pill.
gre.clue: relieved symptoms no better than a sugar pill

example: Across much of Africa, cheap insecticide-treated bed nets rank among the most efficacious tools public health workers have against malaria.

en: To decorate; to add details, often untrue, to make a story more interesting
hook: EMBELLISH: add BELLS to it, decorate.
story: Embellish. Every time Kamal told the story of the snake in his village pond, it grew. First it was a small water snake. A year later it was six feet long. By the time he told it at the hostel, it was a cobra that had chased him up a coconut tree. Kamal embellished the story: he added exciting details that were not true. To embellish also means to decorate, like embellishing a sari with embroidery. Synonyms: embroider, exaggerate, adorn.

gre.s: The journalist was dismissed when editors discovered her habit of choosing to ____ her reports with vivid quotations that no source had ever actually spoken.
gre.clue: vivid quotations that no source had ever actually spoken

example: The job candidate embellished his résumé, turning a two-week internship into a year of senior management experience.

en: Wide-ranging and thorough, covering almost every part of a subject
hook: ENCYCLOPEDIC: like an ENCYCLOPEDIA, knows everything.
story: Encyclopedic. Ask Rafi's uncle about any cricket match since 1985, and he will tell you the runs scored, the balls faced, the umpire's name, the weather, and what he ate while watching it. Last Eid, a cousin tried to stump him with an obscure question about a 1992 match in Sharjah. He answered in three seconds, with details. His cricket knowledge is encyclopedic: comprehensive, covering an enormous range of facts, like an encyclopedia.

gre.s: The guide's ____ knowledge of the city, extending from medieval architecture to the history of every street name, delighted the tourists.
gre.clue: extending from medieval architecture to the history of every street name

example: Professor Haque's encyclopedic grasp of Bengali folk music lets him name the district where almost any song began.

en: Making a wrong seem less serious; partially excusing
hook: EXTENUATING: makes the guilt more TENUOUS (thin).
story: Extenuating. Rafi missed his final exam, and the rules said that meant failing the course. But that morning his father had suffered a heart attack, and Rafi had rushed him to the hospital. The exam committee accepted these extenuating circumstances and allowed him a makeup exam. Extenuating means making a wrong seem less serious; partly excusing it. It comes from the Latin for making thin: such circumstances thin out the blame. Synonyms: mitigating, excusing, palliating.

gre.s: Although the judge acknowledged that the defendant had stolen the medicine, she cited ____ circumstances, noting that he had done so to save his dying child.
gre.clue: he had done so to save his dying child

example: The school accepted that a burst water pipe in the exam hall was an extenuating factor and allowed the students to resit.

en: Joking at the wrong moment about things that are serious
hook: FACETIOUS: makes funny FACES at serious things.
story: Facetious. At a serious meeting about rising dropout rates, the principal asked for ideas. Zubair raised his hand and suggested they simply cancel exams, so that nobody could ever fail. A few teachers smiled; the principal did not. His remark was facetious: treating a serious issue with inappropriate humor. Facetious is joking at the wrong moment. A handy trick: facetious contains all five vowels, a, e, i, o, u, in order, as neat as a joke. Synonyms: flippant, glib, tongue-in-cheek.

gre.s: The minister's ____ remark about the flood victims, which he apparently intended as a joke, provoked outrage among families who had lost everything.
gre.clue: which he apparently intended as a joke

example: Asked how the company would repay its debts, the chief executive gave a facetious reply about winning the lottery.

en: Not perfect, and so sometimes wrong or mistaken
hook: FALLIBLE: able to FALL into error.
story: Fallible. Doctor Ahmed had practised medicine for thirty years. When a junior doctor questioned his diagnosis, he listened, ordered another test, and discovered he had been wrong. He thanked her. "Experience makes you better, but never perfect. Every doctor is fallible." Fallible means capable of making mistakes. It shares a root with fail and false. Its opposite, infallible, means incapable of error. Human memory is notoriously fallible. Synonyms: imperfect, error-prone, unreliable.

gre.s: Eyewitness testimony, once treated as nearly conclusive, is now known to be highly ____, since memories can be distorted by stress, suggestion, and the passage of time.
gre.clue: memories can be distorted by stress, suggestion, and the passage of time

example: Even the most advanced weather models are fallible, so farmers in Rangpur still watch the sky before sowing.

en: A deceptive movement meant to distract an opponent
hook: FEINT: a FAKE move. Sounds like FAINT but means FAKE.
story: Feint. In the final minute of the inter-hall football match, Shuvo dribbled toward the goal. He dropped his shoulder to the left as if to shoot. The goalkeeper dived left. Shuvo calmly rolled the ball into the right corner. That shoulder drop was a feint: a deceptive movement meant to distract an opponent. Boxers feint with one hand before striking with the other. Feint sounds like faint, and the goalkeeper nearly fainted when he realised he had been fooled. Synonyms: ruse, bluff, decoy.

gre.s: The general's apparent retreat was merely a ____: while the enemy rushed to pursue, his main force circled behind them and attacked their unguarded camp.
gre.clue: while the enemy rushed to pursue, his main force circled behind them

example: The chess master's queen move looked like an attack but was only a feint to pull the defending pieces out of position.

en: Socially awkward; lacking grace or tact
hook: GAUCHE: French for LEFT, as in left-handed and clumsy.
story: Gauche. At his first office party, Farhan asked his boss's wife how old she was, laughed loudly at the wrong moment, and wiped his hands on the tablecloth. Everyone smiled politely and looked away. His behaviour was gauche: socially awkward, lacking grace or tact. Gauche is French for left, from an old prejudice that the left hand is clumsy. Its opposite, adroit, comes from the French for right. Synonyms: awkward, tactless, maladroit.

gre.s: Though brilliant in the laboratory, the young chemist was painfully ____ at receptions, blurting out tactless remarks and forgetting the names of her hosts.
gre.clue: blurting out tactless remarks

example: As a gauche teenager, I once congratulated a guest on her pregnancy when she was simply wearing a loose dress.

en: Looking or feeling sad and gloomy
hook: GLUM: GLOOMY + DUMB-struck.
story: Glum. When Bangladesh lost a cricket match in the final over, a match they should have won, the whole tea stall went silent. Men stared into their cups. Nobody argued, nobody joked, and someone switched off the radio. Their faces were glum: sad and gloomy. Glum is a short, heavy word for a short, heavy mood. A glum expression, a glum forecast. Think of glum as gloom with the life squeezed out. Synonyms: morose, dejected, downcast. Opposite: cheerful.

gre.s: Despite the company's record profits, the shareholders' meeting was strangely ____, since everyone knew the beloved founder would announce his resignation.
gre.clue: since everyone knew the beloved founder would announce his resignation

example: The glum faces of the waiting passengers told me that the flight to Cox's Bazar had been delayed yet again.

en: Rude and disrespectful; not showing proper respect
hook: IM-PERTINENT: not pertinent (relevant), and rude to boot.
story: Impertinent. Professor Haque returned the essays. Rafi had received a B. He raised his hand and said, loud enough for everyone to hear, "Maybe you did not understand my essay, sir." The whole class gasped. The professor raised one eyebrow and said nothing for a long, terrible moment. Rafi's remark was impertinent: rude and disrespectful, especially toward someone in authority. Its older meaning is irrelevant, but the GRE usually means rudeness.

gre.s: The young reporter's ____ questions about the senator's private life drew a sharp rebuke from the press secretary.
gre.clue: drew a sharp rebuke

example: The impertinent customer told the elderly tailor that he was far too old to understand modern fashion.

en: Never tiring; persistently energetic
hook: IN-DE-FATIGABLE: cannot be FATIGUED.
story: Indefatigable. During the floods in Sylhet, a young relief worker named Tania worked eighteen hours a day for three weeks. She carried rice sacks on her back, rowed boats through flooded villages, comforted crying mothers, and still smiled at the volunteers every night. Nobody ever saw her tired. She was indefatigable: tireless, incapable of being worn out. In means not, fatigable means able to be fatigued. Fatigue never catches an indefatigable person.

gre.s: Even in her nineties, the ____ activist continued to march at every protest, outlasting colleagues half her age.
gre.clue: outlasting colleagues half her age

example: The indefatigable archivist spent twelve years cataloguing every letter in the old zamindar family's collection.

en: Impossible to understand or interpret
hook: IN-SCRUTABLE: can't be SCRUTINIZED.
story: Inscrutable. At the national poker tournament, the final player sat absolutely still. No smile. No frown. No twitch. Not even a blink. Opponents studied his face for clues and found nothing. Was he holding a perfect hand or bluffing with nothing at all? He won the tournament without anyone ever reading him. His face was inscrutable: impossible to understand or interpret. In means not, scrutable means able to be scrutinized. Synonym: enigmatic.

gre.s: The cat's ____ expression gave no hint of whether it was about to purr contentedly or lash out with its claws.
gre.clue: gave no hint

example: The ancient Indus script remains inscrutable, since no one has yet found a bilingual inscription that would help decode it.

en: To throw away or abandon something unwanted
hook: JETTISON: a JET dumping fuel to lighten its load.
story: Jettison. Halfway up the steep road to Sajek, the overloaded jeep began to stall. The driver ordered everyone out and made them throw away the heavy extras: a crate of soft drinks, two broken plastic chairs, and an old speaker. The lighter jeep climbed easily. They had jettisoned the extra weight. To jettison is to throw away or abandon something unwanted. Sailors once jettisoned cargo to save sinking ships. Companies jettison failing plans. Synonyms: discard, abandon, scrap.

gre.s: Faced with mounting losses, the company decided to ____ its least profitable divisions so that it could focus its resources on its core business.
gre.clue: so that it could focus its resources on its core business

example: The design team jettisoned their original logo after customers said it looked like a broken umbrella.

en: Lacking energy; relaxed and slow
hook: LANGUID: LANGUISHING, lazy.
story: Languid. On a hot Friday afternoon in May, after a heavy lunch of rice and beef curry, the whole family lay on the floor under the ceiling fan. Nobody wanted to talk, read, or move. Even the cat stretched slowly and closed its eyes. The mood was languid: lacking energy, relaxed and slow. Languid can be pleasant, like a languid stroll by the river, or a sign of weakness. Related words are languish and languor. Synonyms: listless, sluggish, lethargic.

gre.s: The afternoon heat made everyone ____: even the usually restless children lay on the cool floor, too sluggish to play or even talk.
gre.clue: too sluggish to play or even talk

example: The cat stretched languidly across the warm windowsill, ignoring the pigeons that strutted just outside the glass.

en: To lose strength; to suffer from being in an unpleasant situation
bn: দুর্বল হয়ে পড়া; কষ্টে দিন কাটানো
hook: LANGUISH: become LANGUID, weak and fading.
story: Languish. A young activist was arrested and held without trial. Months turned into years. In a cramped cell he grew thin and pale, while his case file gathered dust in a government office. He languished in prison: he suffered in an unpleasant situation and slowly lost strength. Plants languish without water; projects languish without funding. Languish shares a root with languid, meaning weak and slow. Synonyms: wither, decline, waste away.

gre.s: Without fresh investment, the once thriving port continued to ____, its warehouses empty and its docks slowly crumbling into the harbor.
gre.clue: its warehouses empty and its docks slowly crumbling

example: Plans for the new metro line languished in government files for twenty years before construction finally began.

en: A person who freely indulges in pleasures, ignoring moral restraints
hook: LIBERTINE: takes too many LIBERTIES with morality.
story: Libertine. In countless old Bengali films, the landlord's spoilt son wastes his inheritance on gambling, drinking, and parties that last until dawn. He laughs at his mother's warnings and mocks every rule the village holds sacred. He is a libertine: a person who freely indulges in pleasures, ignoring moral restraints. Libertine shares a root with liberty, but it means liberty with no self-control. Synonyms: rake, debauchee, hedonist, playboy. Opposites: puritan, ascetic.

gre.s: Unlike his brother, a notorious ____ who squandered his fortune on drink and gambling, the younger prince lived a life of strict self-discipline.
gre.clue: squandered his fortune on drink and gambling

example: Lord Byron was known in London society as a libertine whose love affairs and debts fed endless gossip.

en: An artistic work imitating the style of other works; a medley
hook: PASTICHE: a PASTE of different styles glued together.
story: Pastiche. Lamia's first novel opened like a Humayun Ahmed story, had a middle chapter that read like Tagore, and ended in the style of Agatha Christie. One reviewer called it a clever pastiche: a work that imitates the styles of other works. A pastiche can be a playful tribute, or a criticism meaning a jumble with no voice of its own. It comes from the Italian pasticcio, a pie that mixes many ingredients. Synonyms: imitation, medley, hodgepodge.

gre.s: Critics dismissed the film as a mere ____, cobbled together from scenes borrowed from a dozen earlier thrillers and lacking any style of its own.
gre.clue: cobbled together from scenes borrowed from a dozen earlier thrillers

example: The new shopping mall is an odd pastiche of Greek columns, Mughal domes and mirrored glass towers.

en: A particular fondness for something over other things
hook: PRE-DILECTION: PRE-selected as your DELIGHT.
story: Predilection. Mitu puts green chili on everything: in her eggs, in her noodles, on her mango slices, even, once, on ice cream. Her friends cry when they share her food. She just smiles and adds more. She has a predilection for spicy food: a strong preference or liking. Predilection usually describes a taste or fondness, while proclivity often suggests a bad tendency. Think: pre-selected as your delight.

gre.s: The collector's ____ for small Dutch landscapes was well known, and dealers saved such paintings especially for him.
gre.clue: dealers saved such paintings especially for him

example: The physicist had a predilection for old detective novels, which she read on every long flight to conferences.

en: To finally agree after refusing; to become less severe
hook: RELENT: finally LET it go.
story: Relent. For a whole week, Joya begged her parents to let her join the university trip to Bandarban. Her father said no, again and again, worried about the hill roads. Then her teacher called and promised to watch over the group personally. Finally her father relented: he agreed after refusing. Relent can also mean to become less severe: by evening, the rain relented. Its adjective is relentless, meaning never stopping or softening. Synonyms: give in, soften, yield.

gre.s: The authorities refused for months to release the detained journalist, but mounting international pressure eventually forced them to ____.
gre.clue: refused for months

example: The heavy rain finally relented around noon, and the groundsmen hurried to pull the covers off the pitch.

en: Curving and bending, often in a smooth, graceful way
hook: SINUOUS: like a SNAKE's S-curves.
story: Sinuous. From a plane window over Bangladesh, Kamal watched a river winding across the land in great loops and curves, bending back on itself like a silver snake. Its course was sinuous: full of curves and turns. The word also describes graceful, flowing movement, like a classical dancer's sinuous arms. It comes from the Latin sinus, a curve or fold. Do not confuse it with sinewy, which means muscular and tough. Synonyms: winding, serpentine, meandering.

gre.s: Unlike the straight highways of the plains, the mountain road was ____, twisting back on itself so many times that several passengers grew carsick.
gre.clue: twisting back on itself so many times

example: The dancer's sinuous arm movements made the old Manipuri dance look as smooth as flowing water.

en: To take someone's place, often by plotting or force
hook: SUP-PLANT: uproot one PLANT and put another in its place.
story: Supplant. For decades the pedal rickshaw ruled Dhaka's narrow lanes. Then battery-powered auto-rickshaws arrived, faster and cheaper, and slowly pushed the old rickshaws off route after route. In some neighbourhoods they have supplanted them entirely: replaced them and taken their place. Supplant often suggests replacing by force or scheming. The Latin root means to trip someone up by the heel and then take their spot. Synonyms: replace, oust, displace.

gre.s: The ambitious deputy spent years flattering the board and quietly undermining his superior, plotting all the while to ____ her as head of the company.
gre.clue: quietly undermining his superior

example: The young striker gradually supplanted the veteran captain in the starting eleven, scoring in nine straight matches.

en: Empty of real ideas or intelligence; blank
hook: VACUOUS: like a VACUUM, empty inside.
story: Vacuous. A television host asked a celebrity what she thought about climate change. She smiled and said, "I think the climate is really important, and change is good, so it is all very positive." Viewers laughed. Her answer was vacuous: showing a lack of thought or intelligence; empty. It comes from the same root as vacuum and vacant: nothing inside. A vacuous stare is a blank, empty one. Synonyms: inane, vapid, mindless.

gre.s: The candidate's speeches, full of rousing slogans but devoid of any concrete policy proposals, struck most serious analysts as ____.
gre.clue: devoid of any concrete policy proposals

example: The quiz contestant gave a vacuous grin when asked to name the capital of Australia.

en: Offering nothing stimulating or challenging; dull and empty
hook: VAPID: like VAPOR, empty air.
story: Vapid. The TV channel interviewed a famous actor for twenty minutes. Every answer was the same: "I just love my fans." "I am so blessed." "It was an amazing experience." Not one thought, not one opinion, not one interesting detail. Viewers switched channels. The interview was vapid: dull, empty, and lacking anything stimulating. Think of vapour: just empty air. Vapid is a close synonym of insipid.

gre.s: The critic dismissed the pop song's lyrics as ____, a string of empty phrases that said nothing at all about love.
gre.clue: a string of empty phrases that said nothing at all

example: The award show's vapid speeches, all thanks and no ideas, sent half the audience back to their phones.
